q1.attribution: —Historian's account of the global silver trade, 1550–1700
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern of the silver trade described in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of China's enormous demand for silver.
parts.c: Explain ONE effect of the silver trade on the Spanish Empire.

sample_answers.a: Silver mined at Potosí flowed in two directions — across the Atlantic to Seville and across the Pacific via Manila to China — making it the first globally traded commodity.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the Ming dynasty's tax reforms, which required taxes to be paid in silver, creating a vast state-driven demand that made silver worth more in China than anywhere else.
sample_answers.c: One effect was inflation and dependency: the flood of American silver enriched the Spanish crown in the short term but discouraged domestic industry and left Spain dependent on colonial revenue to fund its European wars.

q1.stimulus: Historians argue that the world economy was born in the 1570s, when a truly global trade in silver linked Potosí, Seville, and Beijing. Spanish America produced the silver; China absorbed it, because the Ming tax system demanded payment in silver and Chinese buyers valued the metal more highly than Europeans did. Silver flowed west across the Atlantic to Spain and east across the Pacific on the Manila galleons — the first commodity traded on a planetary scale.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Smith makes in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the events Smith describes transformed European commerce.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of Smith's celebration of these events.

sample_answers.a: Smith claims that the European discovery of America and the sea route to Asia were the two most important events in recorded human history.
sample_answers.b: The events he describes redirected global commerce onto oceanic routes controlled by Europeans, bringing American silver and Asian goods into European markets and shifting economic power toward Atlantic states.
sample_answers.c: Smith writes from the perspective of European commerce and ignores the cost: the 'discovery' meant conquest, enslavement, and demographic catastrophe for Native peoples — a price his celebration of trade does not acknowledge.

q2.stimulus: The discovery of America, and that of a passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope, are the two greatest and most important events recorded in the history of mankind.

q3.attribution: Colonial-era painting of the Cerro Rico (Rich Hill) of Potosí
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the mining operation suggested by the image.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the Potosí mines depended on coerced labor.
parts.c: Explain ONE environmental consequence of the silver mining shown in the image.

sample_answers.a: The image shows an entire mountain honeycombed with mine entrances, with workers, ore-processing mills, and a town built around the extraction — industrial-scale mining.
sample_answers.b: The mines ran on the mita draft-labor system, which forced Native communities to send workers for brutal underground shifts; the mercury amalgamation process also poisoned workers and the surrounding land.
sample_answers.c: One consequence was severe deforestation, as the mines and refining mills consumed entire forests for timber and fuel, stripping the Andean highlands around Potosí.

q3.stimulus: Colonial-era painting of the Cerro Rico (Rich Hill) of Potosí, in present-day Bolivia — the silver mountain whose mines produced the bulk of the world's silver in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
